attrs.why: Fever, shoulder pain, recent URI, reduced heart sounds/tachycardia, effusion support infectious/inflammatory pericarditis.
Fever/effusion can fit systemic inflammatory disease, but no arthralgia/abdominal pain and clear recent URI favor infection instead.
Fever and effusion could occur with malignancy/TB, but rare and no weight loss/night sweats or other supportive evidence exists.
Ibuprofen exposure after URI may rarely cause effusion; fever and URI also fit infection, so medication reaction is lower priority.

attrs.why: Infectious pericarditis remains most likely. Fever, left shoulder pain, recent URI, reduced cardiac sounds, tachycardia, and moderate pericardial effusion are supported by leukocytosis, high CRP/ESR, and ECG PR depression/ST elevation. Negative TB/viral/ANA tests weaken alternative causes. Confidence stays 0.78 because pericardial fluid culture is pending.

Systemic inflammatory disease remains possible. NLRP12 mutation and IL-1β elevation suggest autoinflammation, adding some support. However, absence of arthralgia/abdominal pain, negative ANA, and a clear recent URI make infection more likely, so confidence is low at 0.15.
Neoplastic/TB effusion is very unlikely. Negative TB tests, no weight loss or night sweats, and no other supportive evidence argue against it, lowering confidence to 0.03.
Ibuprofen-associated effusion is unlikely. No NSAID history or drug-reaction evidence is available, and the recent URI plus inflammatory findings better fit infection, lowering confidence to 0.04.

attrs.why: Current frontier is 'Infectious pericarditis' (too general). Leukocytosis (node-11), high CRP/ESR (node-12), fever (node-3), moderate effusion (node-16), and pending pericardial fluid culture (belief) support a bacterial etiology. Negative viral tests (node-14) may increase relative likelihood of bacterial infection.

Current frontier is 'Infectious pericarditis' (too general). Recent upper respiratory infection (node-6), fever (node-3), ECG PR depression/ST elevation (node-13), and moderate effusion (node-16) are compatible with viral pericarditis, the most common cause in adolescents. However, negative viral tests (node-14) lower this hypothesis.

Current frontier is 'Infectious pericarditis' (too general). Recent URI (node-6) and adolescent age could fit Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a common atypical pathogen that can cause pericarditis. No specific Mycoplasma test result is available in the belief/graph.

Current frontier is 'Infectious pericarditis' (too general). Moderate effusion (node-16) and high ESR (node-12) could suggest TB, but negative TB tests (node-14) and absence of weight loss/night sweats make it unlikely; still considered as a subcategory of infectious pericarditis.

attrs.why: Laboratory expert analysis reports neutrophilia and concludes probable bacterial pericarditis, strengthening the infectious pericarditis hypothesis. Negative TB/viral/ANA tests and exclusion of autoimmune/drug causes further support infection. Confidence increased from 0.78 to 0.86; pericardial fluid culture and procalcitonin remain pending.

Pericardial fluid culture, blood culture, and procalcitonin are pending. Confidence increased from 0.32 to 0.62.
Expert analysis supports bacterial rather than viral etiology and notes negative viral tests. Recent URI and ECG changes are nonspecific. Confidence decreased from 0.28 to 0.12.
Expert analysis supports probable bacterial pericarditis and no Mycoplasma-specific evidence is available. Recent URI could fit but is insufficient. Confidence decreased from 0.10 to 0.05.
Expert analysis excludes TB; negative TB tests and absent weight loss/night sweats argue against tuberculous pericarditis. Confidence decreased from 0.05 to 0.02.

A recent upper respiratory tract infection preceded fever and pericardial effusion, and laboratory expert analysis supports probable bacterial pericarditis with neutrophilia and high inflammatory markers. Negative viral/TB/ANA tests weaken alternative etiologies, but no organism has been identified, so confidence is 0.50 pending pericardial fluid culture.

attrs.why: Both the laboratory physician and the radiologist independently favor an infectious process, specifically bacterial pericarditis, based on fever, moderate pericardial effusion, leukocytosis with neutrophilia, markedly elevated CRP/ESR, and PR depression/ST elevation, together with negative TB, viral, and ANA tests. This convergent specialist agreement and the exclusion of autoimmune, drug, and tuberculous causes strengthen the infectious pericarditis hypothesis, raising confidence from 0.86 to 0.87; pericardial fluid culture, blood culture, and procalcitonin remain pending.

Expert analysis excludes autoimmune causes and supports infection; negative ANA and absence of arthralgia/abdominal pain argue against systemic inflammatory disease. NLRP12 mutation and IL-1β elevation are nonspecific. Confidence decreased from 0.15 to 0.08.

Expert analysis excludes drug causes; no drug-reaction evidence is present, and infection better explains the findings. Confidence decreased from 0.04 to 0.01.

attrs.why: The neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 19,670/µL), high CRP/ESR, moderate effusion with ECG PR depression/ST elevation, recent upper respiratory infection, and negative viral/TB/ANA studies are consistent with bacterial pericarditis, and both the laboratory physician and the radiologist endorse this as the most likely diagnosis. Confidence increased from 0.62 to 0.65, still limited because pericardial fluid culture, blood culture, and procalcitonin have not yet identified an organism.
Expert analysis supports bacterial rather than viral etiology and notes negative viral tests. Recent URI and ECG changes are nonspecific. Confidence decreased from 0.28 to 0.12.
Expert analysis supports probable bacterial pericarditis and no Mycoplasma-specific evidence is available. Recent URI could fit but is insufficient. Confidence decreased from 0.10 to 0.05.
Expert analysis excludes TB; negative TB tests and absent weight loss/night sweats argue against tuberculous pericarditis. Confidence decreased from 0.05 to 0.02.

A recent upper respiratory tract infection preceded the fever and pericardial effusion, and both experts support a probable bacterial pericarditis on the basis of the neutrophilic inflammatory profile, high CRP/ESR, and moderate effusion. This post-URI temporal relationship makes a post-upper-respiratory-infection bacterial pericarditis plausible, raising confidence from 0.50 to 0.52 pending organism confirmation.
